glossary: Here: a directory of what public bodies make and run that others can adopt. Unlike a mobile store it sells nothing and shows no ratings.
One product in the store, with its owner, licence, code, live service and sourced facts.
A listing written by the editor from public sources because the project has no publiccode.yml yet.
A listing read automatically from a project's publiccode.yml file during the weekly harvest.
A public body that has said, through the issue form, that it uses a product. The hub never infers use.
A metadata file placed at the root of a public software repository so catalogues can discover it.
The publiccode.yml field for maturity: concept, development, beta, stable or obsolete.
How ready a product is to adopt. The hub shows only what the owner declares; otherwise 'Not declared'.
A shared service, such as GOV.UK Notify or GOV.UK Pay, that many services use instead of building their own.
Code published under a licence that lets anyone use, change and share it.
A short permissive open source licence.
A copyleft licence: changed versions you distribute must stay under the GPL.
A Creative Commons licence for content: reuse freely with attribution.
The 14 points that government services are assessed against.
The criteria government uses to design, build and buy technology.
The editor's weekly review of submitted and claimed listings before they are published.
The hub's assistant. It searches only the hub's own content and shows where each answer came from.
user_needs: As someone building a public service, I need to find what other public bodies already run, so that I do not build it again.
As someone choosing a product, I need maturity, licence and code links in one place, so that I can judge whether I can adopt it.
As a public body, I need to list or claim my product without writing code, so that others can find it.
As a reader, I need every figure to show its source, so that I can trust and check it.
As the editor, I need the hub to run itself in under an hour a week, so that one person can sustain it.
As anyone, I need the hub to work on a phone, with a keyboard or a screen reader, in light or dark, so that I can use it.
requirements: Show every listing with owner, licence, code and live links
Filter and sort listings by category, body type, kind and licence
Show maturity only as declared; otherwise 'Not declared'
Never show star ratings or reviews
Every figure cites a known source with an https address
Harvest publiccode.yml weekly and open a pull request with changes
List or claim a product through a GitHub issue form, never by email
Search across the whole hub and an Ask assistant grounded in hub content
Retractable left drawer with a labelled toggle inside it; folding global navigation
No horizontal scroll at 400px; light and dark themes; reduced motion respected
Link to existing directories instead of copying them
Publish the reconciliation register for the Figma prototype
Show the editor's weekly effort and the running costs openly
Show who declares use of each listing, as each body declares it
defects: Prototype carried invented figures (342 apps, 58M+ users, star ratings)
The prototype was a design mock with no data sources
Every listing figure must cite a known source; ratings fields are rejected
Email pattern check on the page and on every data value, including harvested publiccode.yml contacts
Prototype footer said the portal was operated by CDDO and used Crown branding
Check for retired or misleading names and Crown marks
Prototype listed a political party as a think tank
Ecosystem lists hold only names and official https links, with no labels that classify organisations
On a phone, opening a deep link such as #store hid the page heading under the sticky masthead
The browser's own anchor jump ran after the page reset its scroll position
Reset the scroll after the anchor jump; the visual inspection opens a deep link and checks the heading is visible
With the drawer closed, its toggle showed only a switch with no visible label
The label was hidden with the drawer contents
Keep the label visible in the closed rail; the visual inspection checks it
Repulsion too weak for the number of nodes
Stronger spacing; the graph is also given as a text list for anyone who cannot use it
The first sync failed: CI said the built site was out of date although it had just been built
The QR code library writes '/>' or ' />' depending on whether lxml is installed, so the build differed between machines
Normalise the QR code markup; a unit test checks it, and the build check now reports where the page differs
On phones the page scrolled sideways in CI, though not on the build machine
The masthead could not shrink with the wider fonts on CI's Linux runner, and the colophon barcode kept millimetre units inside its viewBox, so its bars spilled 3.8 times wider than the box

The masthead text now shrinks and the subtitle hides on small screens; the barcode uses plain units and clips; the visual inspection now uses a wide fallback font, adds a 360px width and names the element that sticks out
On phones the closed drawer rail covered the left edge of the footer text
The rail is fixed to the left of the screen; the main column was padded for it but the footer was not
Pad the footer on small screens too; the visual inspection checks the closed rail does not overlap the footer
